group.passage: Over the past few decades, allergies such as hay fever and asthma have become far more common in wealthy countries. In the two texts below, a researcher looks back at a famous theory about why, and a doctor who treats allergic children adds a word of caution.

passage_parts.label: A
passage_parts.title: A Theory Born in Crowded Homes
passage_parts.text: In 1989, a British doctor, David Strachan, noticed something curious while studying data on thousands of children: those who had several older brothers and sisters were less likely to suffer from hay fever. He suggested that the infections passed around in large families might teach a young immune system to tell real threats from harmless substances such as pollen. Smaller families and cleaner homes, in his view, could leave that lesson unfinished, and his theory became known as the “hygiene hypothesis.” Later research added an important twist. Children who grow up on traditional farms, in daily contact with animals and barn dust, are also far less likely to develop asthma and allergies. Many scientists now think that what matters is not infection itself but regular contact with a wide range of harmless microbes, the tiny living things in soil, in animals and in our own bodies that humans have lived alongside for most of their history.

passage_parts.label: B
passage_parts.title: Keep the Soap
passage_parts.text: As a doctor who treats allergic children, I welcome this research, but I wish the theory had been given a different name. The word “hygiene” leads many parents to conclude that keeping clean is itself the problem, and some have even stopped washing their children’s hands. They are barking up the wrong tree. Washing hands removes the germs that cause serious infections; it does very little to the friendly microbes the research is really about, most of which we meet outdoors, in food and through other people. My advice, then, is simple. Keep up handwashing before meals and after using the toilet, but also let children play in parks and gardens, get their hands muddy and spend time with animals. And remember that allergies have many causes, from the genes we inherit to the air we breathe, so no single habit can guarantee an allergy-free child.

translation_zh.text:
過去幾十年來，花粉熱、氣喘等過敏疾病在富裕國家變得常見許多。在下面兩篇短文中，一位研究者回顧一個解釋原因的著名理論，一位治療過敏兒童的醫師則提出提醒。

A　誕生於擁擠家庭的理論
1989 年，英國醫師大衛．史特拉肯在研究數千名兒童的資料時注意到一件奇怪的事：有好幾個哥哥姊姊的孩子比較不容易得花粉熱。他提出，在大家庭裡互相傳染的疾病，也許能教會年幼的免疫系統分辨真正的威脅和花粉之類無害的物質。在他看來，家庭變小、家裡變乾淨，可能會讓這堂課沒上完；他的理論後來被稱為「衛生假說」。後來的研究帶來了重要的轉折：在傳統農場長大、每天接觸動物和穀倉塵土的孩子，得到氣喘和過敏的可能性也低得多。許多科學家現在認為，重要的不是感染本身，而是經常接觸各式各樣無害的微生物——也就是存在於土壤、動物和我們自己身體裡，人類在大部分歷史中一直與之共同生活的微小生物。

B　肥皂別丟
身為治療過敏兒童的醫師，我很歡迎這項研究，但我真希望這個理論當初取了別的名字。「衛生」這個詞讓許多父母以為保持乾淨本身就是問題，有些人甚至不再幫孩子洗手。他們完全找錯了方向。洗手能去除造成嚴重感染的病菌；它對這些研究真正關心的友善微生物幾乎沒有影響，而這些微生物大多是我們在戶外、從食物中、透過其他人接觸到的。所以我的建議很簡單：飯前便後要繼續洗手，但也要讓孩子在公園和花園裡玩、把手弄得髒兮兮的，並和動物相處。還要記得，過敏有許多成因，從我們遺傳到的基因到我們呼吸的空氣都是，所以沒有任何單一習慣能保證孩子不過敏。
